## A Thursday afternoon with the tea trolley

The bourbon biscuits always go first. This is one of the things I have learnt since joining the Thursday tea trolley at Wensum Vale Hospice. We now keep a packet back for the late group. Otherwise, they don’t stand a chance.

I started in March 2022, eighteen months after retiring from 41 years of bookkeeping, mostly for a builders’ merchant in Dereham. I had looked forward to retirement, but found that without work I often had no regular reason to go out. I drifted a bit. Thursdays gave me something definite to put in the diary, and people who expected me to turn up.

I wasn’t entirely sure what to expect of the hospice. If you are thinking that volunteering here must be terribly sad, or that you would need some sort of nursing qualification, I can understand it. I wondered much the same myself.

On my first afternoon, I spilled an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much that she had to be given a tissue. She told me it was the best afternoon she’d had in a month. I wouldn’t recommend this as an introduction to volunteering, but it did help me stop worrying quite so much about getting everything right.

There are usually about 14 to 18 patients in the day therapy unit on a Thursday. Some come for the art group, some for a hand massage, some for company. Most go home afterwards. It is generally noisy and rather jolly, with plenty of conversation to keep up with as we go round.

Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods each week. The account varies a little from one telling to the next. I have stopped correcting the dates. He enjoys telling it, and I have time to listen.

You don’t need nursing skills to do the tea trolley. You need to be able to push it, remember who takes what, and listen. Forty-one years of keeping ledgers straight turns out to be quite useful for remembering tea orders, though it hasn’t prevented the occasional mistake.

Some weeks are hard. People are ill, and there are sad days. I wouldn’t want to pretend otherwise. But the staff look after us when those days come, and sadness isn’t the whole of an afternoon here. There is also a great deal of ordinary chat over a cup of tea, which I think most of us appreciate.

At present there are four of us on a rota meant for six. Two volunteers left over the summer: one moved to Sheffield to be near the grandchildren, and the other had a knee operation. We could do with a couple more pairs of hands.

The commitment is **one Thursday a fortnight, from 1.30 to 4pm**. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, does the induction, which takes about two hours. There is also a short online food hygiene course, paid for by the hospice. You aren’t simply handed the trolley and left to work it out.

If you think it might suit you, there is a **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits, and no obligation to sign up. Or you can ring Bridget on the volunteering line for a chat.

I’d be very pleased if this persuaded two people to come along and find out a bit more. You don’t have to decide beforehand whether hospice volunteering is for you. I certainly didn’t know until I tried it.
